title: Emotional positioning and intended feelings
definition: A product states, before it designs, which feelings it intends a user to have at which moments (first use, a decision, an error, a result), in which words, and who decided. A feeling in a profile is an INTENDED design target. It is never reported as measured unless evidence of a stronger class exists.
intended_outcome: Every interface decision can be traced to a named intended feeling at a named moment, so design can be reviewed against intent and not only against taste.
implementation_guidance: Record three to five intended feelings in the profile emotional_promise[], each labelled intended with measured:false, each with the journey moments it applies to.

For each key journey (first run, primary task, failure, completion) write one line: at this moment the user should feel X because the interface does Y. Y must name a concrete behaviour: copy, state, layout, motion or timing.
Treat a design rationale of "feels premium" or "feels modern" with no named feeling and moment as an assessment finding.
Where an intended feeling conflicts with a domain duty (reassurance versus a safety or loss-of-money alert), the duty wins; record the case in domain_overrides[].
Do not add a feeling to the profile unless at least one journey moment and one interface behaviour can be named for it.

automated: Profile validator: every emotional_promise item is labelled intended, measured:false, and carries evidence.
expert_review: Walk each key journey and check that each step names a feeling and an interface behaviour that realises it.
customer_feedback: A short post-task question about how the user felt, recorded as customer feedback and never as proof that the design caused the feeling.

limitations: Feelings cannot be read from a repository. The engine can check that intent is declared and traceable, not that users feel it.
Self-reported feeling depends on how and when the question is asked.

evidence.summary: The owner directs that brand strategy is expressed as intended customer feelings in the product experience.
Naming a feeling per journey moment turns a taste argument into a reviewable statement.
evidence.rationale: Untested in Dot products. Reviewers can disagree about a stated feeling, which is the point, but no Dot team has yet shown that it improves outcomes.
